item.title: The Secret Behind Your Dog's Dramatic Sigh
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Sighing in dogs is real, normal, and often meaningful — it is a deeper inhale followed by a slow exhale that brings in extra oxygen, expels carbon dioxide, and helps reset tiny air sacs in the lungs called alveoli
  • The most common reasons dogs sigh includes contentment and relaxation (often paired with a soft face and loose body), pleasure during petting, boredom or frustration, disappointment when something fun ends, and attention seeking
  • A sigh in a tense or unfamiliar setting can be a self-soothing response to anxiety, especially if paired with a tucked tail, flat ears, lip licking, yawning, trembling, or pacing
  • Some sounds that look or sound like sighs actually point to bigger problems: moans can indicate pain, labored breathing involves visible effort with each breath, panting at rest can signal heat or heart issues, and wheezing can mean a blocked airway
  • Occasional sighing is part of normal dog life, but a sudden increase in sighing or sighing paired with changes in appetite, energy, posture, or breathing rate (a healthy dog rests at about 15 to 30 breaths per minute) is worth a quick check-in with your vet

Your dog curls up next to you on the couch, gets comfortable, and lets out a sigh so deep and theatrical it sounds like they have had the longest day of their life. Or they are staring at you from across the room while you finish an email, and you hear that pointed little exhale that feels suspiciously like commentary.

If it sometimes seems like your dog is sighing on purpose, you are not imagining things. Sighing is real, it is normal, and it can mean a surprising number of things depending on the moment. The trick is learning to read the context.

What a Sigh Actually Is

A sigh is a deeper, longer breath than the rhythmic ones your dog takes all day. It usually starts with an audible inhale that runs about twice the length of a normal breath, followed by a slow, pronounced exhale. Sometimes it comes out through the mouth. More often, in dogs, it comes out through the nose with the mouth closed.1

Physiologically, sighing brings in extra oxygen and helps move carbon dioxide out. It is a quiet reset for the respiratory system, and it is something every mammal does. The dramatic version is the one we notice, but plenty of sighs are subtle enough that we miss them entirely.2,3

Sighing Is a Built-In Reflex

Before we get to the emotional reasons, it helps to know that sighing is partly just biology. Dogs (and humans) sigh several times an hour without thinking about it, because those occasional deep breaths help keep the lungs working properly.4

Tiny air sacs in the lungs called alveoli can collapse if they are not stretched open from time to time. A sigh inflates them again, almost like resetting a balloon that has gotten a little floppy. This is happening in the background all day, whether your dog is napping, walking, or staring out the window.5,6

So, a sigh, by itself, is rarely something to read too much into. It is the context around the sigh — the body language, the situation, the timing — that tells the real story.

Sighing May Be a Sign of Contentment and Relaxation

This is probably the version most pet parents recognize. Your dog flops onto their bed, gets settled, and the sigh just rolls out. They are comfortable. They are letting go. They are signaling to their own body, and to you, that everything is okay.

A contented sigh in moments of relaxation is paired with a soft face; closed or half-closed eyes, loose ears and a relaxed tail and body. The mouth may be slightly open and there is no tension present.7,8

Senior dogs especially seem to sigh as they finally find the right position to settle into, which can be a sign that the spot they have chosen feels good. Puppies do their own version too — sometimes a soft sigh, sometimes a tiny groan that means much the same thing.9

Pets Also Sigh During Petting or Play

That sigh you get during a long belly rub, or a slow ear scratch is a close cousin of the contentment sigh. It is your dog telling you that the moment is hitting the spot.

Again, look for that calm body language — a soft face, half-closed eyes, relaxed posture, a loose tail. If your dog leans in, exhales deeply, and stays in place, the sigh is almost certainly a happy one. Learning to read your pet’s body language is one of the most useful skills a pet parent can develop.10

Bored or Frustrated Pets Sigh, Too

Now we move into the more pointed sighs. If you are deep into a work project and your dog is across the room watching you, the sigh you hear might be the canine equivalent of an eye roll. Sometimes this type of sigh can also sound more like a “huff.”

A bored sigh tends to come with alert, open eyes and a body that looks anxious or anticipatory rather than relaxed. Your dog may shift positions, glance at the door, or rest their chin on their paws and stare. The sigh is saying, plainly, "this is not very interesting" or “come on, let’s do something fun.”

Active dogs stuck inside on rainy days are especially prone to sighing out their frustration. A walk, a tug session, a puzzle toy, or a few minutes of indoor training can usually turn that around.

It Can Also Be a Sign of Disappointment

Some dogs sigh when something good comes to an end — the walk is over, the toy is being put away, and the visitor is leaving. The body language looks a lot like the bored sigh: alert eyes, a watchful posture, sometimes a head resting heavily on the floor or a paw.

It is hard to know exactly how much of this is intentional and how much is the body releasing tension as the fun winds down. Either way, it is a sweet, slightly theatrical part of living with a dog who really did love what just happened.

Your Dog May Be Seeking Attention

Dogs are sharper than we give them credit for. If a sigh has ever resulted in you looking up, putting your phone down, or saying "what is it, buddy?” your dog has noticed. Some dogs learn that a well-timed sigh gets a response, and they start using it that way.

This is a pretty harmless habit, and arguably preferable to other attention-getting strategies like chewing the rug or excessive barking. If your dog has trained you to look over when they sigh, well, congratulations to them.

Anxiety or Stress Can Also Trigger a Sigh

A sigh in the waiting room at the vet's office is not the same kind of sigh as the one on the couch. In a tense or unfamiliar environment, sighing can be a sign your dog is trying to self-soothe.

Deep breathing can help dial down stress, and dogs use it the same way we do. The body language will look different from a contented sigh — you may see a tucked tail, ears flat against the head, lip licking, yawning, trembling, pacing, or hypervigilance (when your dog seems on guard even when nothing is actually wrong).

If sighing is paired with these stress signals, the kindest thing you can do is reduce the pressure of the situation — move away from whatever is causing it, give your dog a quiet spot, or work with a trainer on desensitization techniques over time.

Sighing Is Common When a Pet Is in Pain or Discomfort

Sighing is not a classic sign of pain in dogs, but it can sometimes accompany it — especially in senior dogs or dogs with arthritis who are working to find a comfortable position. The sigh you hear when they finally settle down might be relief.

Other signs that a sigh might be tied to discomfort include limping, restlessness, panting at rest, withdrawal from interaction, changes in eating or sleeping or signs of pain such as whimpering or wincing when touched. If you suspect that your pet is in pain, a veterinary exam is the right next step.

One useful tip: If your dog repeatedly sighs while you are cuddling them, sometimes that sigh is a polite version of "I have had enough now." Stiff body, ears that flatten, or an attempt to slide away can confirm it. Letting them have their space goes a long way.

When It Is Not Really a Sigh

A few dog sounds can look or sound like sighs at first glance but actually point to something different — and sometimes more serious. It is worth knowing the difference.11,12

  • Moans come from the vocal cords, not from a deep breath. They can indicate pain or discomfort — abdominal, back, or joint — and warrant a vet visit if they are new or frequent.
  • Panting is many short, rapid breaths rather than one long one. Normal panting cools dogs down or accompanies excitement but panting or breathing heavily at rest in room temperature, or combined with other symptoms such as coughing, lethargy, drooling, or vomiting is a reason to call your vet.
  • Labored breathing involves visible effort with each breath — the chest wall and abdomen (belly) will be working harder than usual with more effort each time they breathe. Unlike a single sigh, it is sustained. If your pet has labored breathing and especially if they are breathing rapidly with over thirty breaths in one minute — this is an emergency and you should see your vet as soon as possible.
  • Wheezing or a high-pitched whistle on breathing can mean a blocked or narrowed airway or a respiratory issue and also needs prompt veterinary attention.
  • Yawns also involve a big inhale, but the mouth opens wide, just like in people. A yawn here and there is normal in dogs; but yawning alongside lip licking, whale eye (the whites of the eyes showing), and a tense body can also mean stress or anxiety.

When to Check in with Your Vet

Occasional sighing is part of being a dog. But if your dog suddenly starts sighing much more than usual, or if sighing shows up with other changes — like rapid or noisy breathing, coughing, decreased appetite, low energy, or a change in behavior — a quick veterinary visit is a sensible step. New or unusual patterns are worth a closer look.

For reference, a healthy dog at rest takes somewhere around 15 to 30 breaths per minute (when they are not panting), with their chest rising and falling rhythmically. Anything that looks substantially different — especially fast breathing while at rest (over thirty breaths per minute); labored, or noisy breathing — deserves a phone call.13,14

Decoding a Sigh Is Easier Than You Think

That dramatic sigh from your dog is one of the most expressive sounds they make, and it almost always means something — even if that something is just a perfectly natural reflex. Most of the time, sighing is a happy, harmless part of dog life: a wind-down after a long walk, a satisfied response to a belly rub, a tiny editorial comment when you are taking too long with dinner.

The secret behind the dramatic sigh is mostly that it is not particularly mysterious. Read the room — the soft face, the alert eyes, the relaxed or tense body language — and you will usually know exactly what your dog is telling you. And on the off chance the sighing changes or comes with other red flags, your vet is the best partner for figuring out the rest.

Sources and References

  • 2,4,6,8 American Kennel Club, June 12, 2025
  • 3,9,11,14 PetMD, July 24, 2024

item.description:
Rory knows tricks, responds to questions, and seems to understand nearly everything her mom says. But her most impressive talent? Spotting bad dates. After one boyfriend earned Rory’s disapproval and turned out to be trouble, her owner learned to trust her cat’s instincts.

item.title: This Misunderstood Farm Animal That's Playful Like a Dog
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Pigs share many cognitive, emotional and personality traits with animals that are considered to be intelligent, such as chimpanzees and dogs
  • Pigs can prioritize important memories, anticipate positive and negative situations, and display spatial learning skills, such as learning how to navigate a maze
  • Pigs demonstrate a form of empathy and are also playful animals, displaying many similar play behaviors as dogs
  • Play is critical to pigs' emotional and cognitive development — insufficient opportunity to explore leads to behavioral abnormalities
  • The Nonhuman Rights Project is petitioning courts to recognize that certain nonhuman animals, including great apes, elephants and dolphins, are entitled to basic legal rights

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published April 26, 2016.

Pigs are easily one of the most misunderstood animal species. They're viewed by many as dirty and useful for little more than a food source — but in fact they're highly intelligent (and among the cleanest domestic animals).

A report published in the International Journal of Comparative Psychology reviewed cognition, emotion and personality in pigs and revealed they share many traits with animals that are considered to be intelligent.1

The findings should have major implications for the industrial livestock industry, which raises pigs on CAFOs (concentrated animal feeding operations) as though they are non-thinking objects, not intelligent beings.

Unfortunately, while it's excellent news that pigs are starting to gain some much-needed recognition, it will likely be some time before the findings permeate through to the livestock industry.

Pigs Are Psychologically Complex Animals

Researchers from Emory University reviewed dozens of studies on pigs and other animals, revealing compelling insights that pigs are psychologically complex. For instance, pigs are highly social animals and use their snouts to engage in behaviors such as rooting, carrying and pushing, and social interactions.

Pigs can also prioritize important memories, such as which site typically contains more food, anticipate positive and negative situations, and display spatial learning skills, such as learning how to navigate a maze.

Pigs are also playful animals and display many similar play behaviors as dogs. Among them, pigs may carry or shake objects such as a ball or stick, toss straw into the air, run playfully, hop around, jump, paw and scamper. They may also engage in play fighting, pushing and running after each other.

Play, it turns out, is extremely important for pigs' emotional and cognitive development. According to the study:2

"So important is this need that insufficient opportunity to explore leads to behavioral abnormalities.
Young pigs reared in a cognitively challenging and complex environment affording greater interactions with objects and other pigs are more socio-cognitively developed than their counterparts raised in standard farrowing crates found that when given access to materials allowing for exploration, pigs engaged in more behaviors associated with positive affect, such as play, and especially locomotor play.
Also, consistent with these findings is the fact that pigs make more optimistic choices (have a positive bias) when in enriched environments than in others, indicating that they find stimulation rewarding and pleasurable.
Therefore, opportunities for play and exploration impact emotional development in pigs as well."

Pig Intelligence Rivals That of Dogs and Chimps

Study co-author and neuroscientist Lori Marino, Ph.D. of Emory University and The Nonhuman Rights Project said in a press release:

"We have shown that pigs share a number of cognitive capacities with other highly intelligent species such as dogs, chimpanzees, elephants, dolphins, and even humans … There is good scientific evidence to suggest we need to rethink our overall relationship to them."

Pigs, it appears, develop sophisticated social behaviors, including competitive behaviors, as seen in some primate species. They are also sensitive to the attentional state of humans, which is also seen in dogs and primates.

For instance, young pigs can utilize human head cues to discriminate between different attention states in humans. They prefer humans who are attentive, and can also distinguish between familiar and unfamiliar humans.

In addition, pigs may show empathy; they not only connect with the emotions of other pigs but also to do so with pigs who are responding emotionally in anticipation of future events. The researchers also revealed that pigs:3

  • Have excellent long-term memories
  • Excel at tests requiring location of objects
  • Comprehend a symbolic language
  • Learn complex combinations of symbols for actions and objects
  • Live in social communities and learn from one another
  • Cooperate with one another
  • Move a joystick to move an on-screen cursor (similar to chimpanzees)
  • Can use a mirror to find hidden food

Should Intelligent Animals Like Pigs Have Rights?

Research into the sentience of pigs raises some important ethical considerations. Most people would agree that chimpanzees, dogs and other intelligent creatures, like elephants and dolphins, deserve some form of protections and rights.

Yet, pigs, which appear to be similarly intelligent, are raised in some of the most inhumane conditions on the planet.

The Nonhuman Rights Project is tackling such issues head on; they're petitioning courts to recognize that existing scientific evidence suggests certain nonhuman animals are entitled to basic legal rights, including bodily liberty and integrity.

In December 2013, the organization filed lawsuits on behalf of four chimpanzees that are imprisoned in New York. The cases, which are moving through the appellate courts, call for the chimps to be freed and transferred to live on a sanctuary.

The group intends to first focus on rights for great apes, elephants, dolphins and whales, "for whom there is clear scientific evidence of such complex cognitive abilities as self-awareness and autonomy."4 It's not a stretch that someday pigs should also be granted some form of protection or at least the ability to live out their days engaging in natural pig behaviors that are currently impossible on CAFOs. It's intriguing work, and this is only the beginning.

Marino and colleagues have also found evidence of cognitive, emotional and social complexity in chickens, and they plan to study other CAFO animals, including cows and goats, in the near future.5

Sources and References

  • 1,2 International Journal of Comparative Psychology 2015, 28
  • 3,5 Discovery News June 11, 2015 (Archived)
  • 4 The Nonhuman Rights Project, Q&A (Archived)

item.title: The Citrus Fruit Pet Parents Always Ask About
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Oranges are OK as dog treats, as they may provide nutrients like vitamin C, flavonoids and other bioactive compounds
  • The vitamin C in oranges may help boost immunity in pets and support collagen production, which is important for joint, skin and coat health
  • Oranges' phytochemical content, like saponins and tannins, may help curb inflammation
  • Feed your dogs a few fresh slices, obviously peeled with the seeds removed
  • Make sure you don’t give them the peel, since it may cause stomach discomfort due to the essential oils it contain

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 2, 2018.

Oranges are one of the most popular fruits in the U.S., ranking in 6th place behind bananas, strawberries, grapes, apples and watermelon.1 While this popularity may be all thanks to their taste and flavor, oranges are also well known for the nutrients they offer. These fruits contain a surplus of bioactive compounds and metabolites crucial for biological processes, such as immune function and collagen production.2

Most people enjoy eating fresh orange slices because of their sweet and refreshing flavor. However, if you suddenly notice your dog eyeing a piece or two, you may be curious if your pet can tolerate this fruit or not.

With its surplus of bioactive components, as well as the health benefits this fruit has to offer, small amounts of fresh oranges can be shared. Oranges can be given to pets as healthy treats (make sure all treats make up less than 10% of their daily caloric intake) or added to their nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet.

Where Do Oranges Grow?

Every year, about 50 million tons of oranges are harvested all around the world. While this fruit is cultivated in different regions, three countries lead the pack in orange production:3

1. Brazil — 15.9 million tons

2. China — 7.5 million tons

3. U.S. — 4.2 million tons

Protect Pets Against Pathogens with Oranges’ Phytochemicals

Researchers from the University of Benin and Kentucky published a study analyzing the phytochemical components of oranges. They found plentiful bioactive compounds, such as flavonoids, tannins, saponins and alkaloids, which lend oranges their antibacterial, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

Optimizing your pet’s diet to include these compounds may help protect them from infections and chronic diseases triggered by constant inflammation.4

Did You Know?

Oranges aren’t found in the wild naturally, since they’re a cross between two citrus fruits: pomelo and mandarin. Oranges got the best of their parent fruits, inheriting the sweetness of the mandarin and the fibrous flesh of the pomelo.5

Boost Your Pet’s Immune System with Vitamin C

"Vitamin C is often regarded as the most important vitamin found in citrus fruits. This antioxidant is linked to the immune system and iron absorption."

For its function in immunity, vitamin C works by boosting both the adaptive and innate immune systems. It is especially important in supporting the epithelial barrier function and skin health — the body’s first line of defense against pathogens.

Vitamin C also figures in collagen production, a component that is not only vital for wound healing and skin health, but is also responsible for decreasing gut permeability and improving microbiota health.6,7 Two tablespoons of orange slices can offer your pet up to 12 milligrams of vitamin C.8

Fun Fact About Oranges

Only 20% of all fruits, including oranges, produced worldwide are sold as fresh fruits. The remaining 80% are typically processed into juice, preserves and extracts.9

How to Feed Oranges to Pets

Remember that misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of overconsumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

As for oranges, you can safely feed your dogs a few fresh slices, obviously peeled with the seeds removed. Just make sure you don’t give them the peel, since it may cause stomach discomfort due to the essential oils it contains. Too many orange slices can cause loose stools if fed in excess. Cats generally have an aversion to all citrus, but a bite of orange is safe for cats (without the peel).

Orange-flavored food or drinks, such as orange juice and canned oranges, shouldn’t be given to pets, since they’re often loaded with added sugars and high-fructose corn syrups, and excessive sugar consumption can be problematic for pets, just as it can be for humans.10

Remember that while oranges and other fresh fruits are healthy, all "extras," including oranges, should be limited to only about 10% of your pet’s daily diet, together with other types of treats. Your pet should be getting the bulk of their nutrients from complete meals, with treats serving as an addition or bonus to nutritionally optimal diets.

Sources and References

  • 2 StatPearls, June 19, 2026
  • 3 USDA, January 2026
  • 4 Clin Phytosci, 6, 46 (2020)
  • 5 TasteMade, 8 Things You Didn’t Know About Oranges (Archived)

  • 7 Nutrients. 2017 Aug 12;9(8):866
  • 8 USDA FoodData Central, Oranges, raw, all commercial varieties
  • 9 Serious Facts, 40 Interesting Orange Facts (Archived)

item.title: Dogs Get This Special Care 5 Times More Often Than Cats, but Why?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Cats in the U.S. don’t make it to the vet’s office nearly as often as their canine counterparts
  • There are many logical reasons to avoid veterinary visits, but the reality is that every cat should see a vet at least once a year
  • It’s important to find a veterinarian who doesn’t push a regular vaccine schedule or unnecessary pest control products, especially for indoor-only cats
  • It’s also important to find a kitty-friendly veterinary practice, or mobile cat practice, one that is either cats-only or follows feline-friendly handling guidelines
  • There are many things you can do as your cat’s primary advocate to improve his or her experience during veterinary visits

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 21, 2017.

If you share your life with a cat and a dog and are like the majority of pet parents, your canine pal sees the vet much more frequently than your cat does. In fact, according to one report, only 1 cat is seen by a veterinarian for every 5 dogs, even though there are several million more pet cats in the U.S. than dogs.1

A pet food company took a survey of over 1,000 cat and dog owners to gauge their “beliefs and motivations,” with the following results:2

  • Compared to dog owners, six times as many cat owners didn’t take their cat to the vet in 2016
  • Two-thirds of cat owners simply believe cats have fewer health issues than dogs
  • The older a cat gets, the more likely the owner is to take her to the vet only when she is sick
  • Thirty-one percent of those with a senior cat only take her to the vet when she is sick, compared to 20% for adult cats, 18% for adolescents and 17% for kittens

The lack of routine feline vet visits worries veterinarians, especially feline practitioners, and cat advocacy groups like the CATalyst Council and others. Their concern is understandable, but so are the reasons kitties don’t make it to the vet’s office all that often, including:

  • Many cats live entirely indoors, so the risk of acquiring an infectious disease or injury is extremely low
  • Cats are notoriously stoic when they don’t feel well, because they’re wired that way, so it’s difficult even for expert cat guardians to tell when kitty is sick
  • Whereas many dogs are rambunctious and accident-prone, cats are naturally cautious and much less likely to court disaster
  • The vast majority of kitties absolutely despise car rides and vet clinics, so for many cat parents, the stress of vet visits seems to outweigh any benefit their pet receives
  • Many conventional veterinarians continue to heavily promote routine re-vaccinations and pest control chemicals (flea/tick, heartworm, etc.) even for indoor-only kitties whose exposure risk is minimal. Many cat guardians don’t agree with that approach and don’t appreciate being pressured

So what’s a conscientious cat parent to do?

Recommendations for Cat Veterinary Visits

First and foremost, try to find a veterinarian whose practice philosophy you’re comfortable with. This may be a holistic or integrative veterinarian, or a conventional veterinarian who doesn’t aggressively promote vaccines, pest preventives or veterinary drugs at every visit.

Alternatively, you’ll need to advocate for your cat with your vet, and push back as necessary, politely but firmly. Keep in mind that you have the final say in what treatments and chemicals are administered to your pet.

Unfortunately, there are still many conventional practitioners who continue to over-vaccinate pets and recommend unnecessary pest control products during routine vet visits. Ideally, twice-yearly wellness visits is recommended for the following three reasons:

  1. Changes in your kitty’s health can happen in a short period of time, especially on the inside where you can’t see it, like sudden changes in kidney health
  2. Sick cats often show no signs of illness, but early detection allows for early intervention
  3. Semi-annual visits give you and your veterinarian the opportunity to closely monitor changes in your kitty’s behavior and attitude that require further investigation

At a minimum, younger healthy cats should see the vet once a year. Kitties over the age of 7 and those with chronic health conditions should be seen twice a year or more frequently if necessary.

Performing regular at-home physical exams on your cat to learn what’s normal and what’s not is also recommended. This will help you stay on top of her health, and if you can only manage an annual visit to your veterinarian, at-home exams will help alert you to changes in her health in between checkups.

Finding a Cat-Friendly Veterinary Clinic

Because veterinary visits are so stressful for cats, find either a cats-only practice or one that actively takes steps to make their feline patients as comfortable and relaxed as possible.

The American Association of Feline Practitioners (AAFP) and the International Society of Feline Medicine (ISFM) created a set of “Feline-Friendly Handling Guidelines”3 that offers suggestions for veterinarians who want to create an inviting environment for their cat patients. These include:

  • Managing clinic odors — Cats are macrosmatic, which means their very acute sense of smell drives them to behave in specific ways. Certain scents, for example, air fresheners, disinfectants and blood, can cause kitties to feel anxious or fearful.
  • Placing synthetic feline facial pheromone (FFP) analog diffusers and sprays throughout the clinic — Research shows these products have a calming effect on cats under stress, and can help reduce anxiety, fear and aggressive responses during vet visits.
  • Reducing what feline patients see and hear during visits — Keeping other people and pets out of a cat's line of sight can alleviate anxiety. If the clinic is able to provide a separate entrance and waiting room for cats, even better. Noisy environments, including loud voices, should be avoided.

    Ask the receptionist if you can wait in your car with your cat if you feel the waiting room is anything less than serene. If your cat needs to be hospitalized, ask that she be housed away from dogs and loud environments.

    Vets who treat cats and their staffs should know how to safely and effectively manage every type of kitty, from the most docile to the most “fractious” (aggressive).

    Very aggressive cats may be best managed by breathing in sevoflurane gas (similar to the “laughing gas” used for highly stressed dental patients) to reduce anxiety.

    Believe it or not, one client has an aggressive cat who comes in his own travel box (a clear Rubbermaid tub), which she equipped with two small holes that allow for oxygen and inhalant gas to be easily administered.

    This dramatically reduces stress on the cat, the cat’s owner and the entire veterinary staff because kitty’s happy coming in, happy going under and happy going home!

If you aren't comfortable with how your cat is treated or handled during vet visits, it's up to you to advocate for your kitty with the vet and staff, or find another practice more attuned to the special needs of feline patients. The least stressful way to make sure your cat is healthy without traveling at all is to consider calling a mobile vet clinic to visit your home.

Not every city or town has the luxury of a mobile veterinary service, and not every cat parent can afford the extra expense, but this is recommended for highly stressed cats when it makes sense.

5 More Tips for Better Vet Visits

  1. Do some dry runs to the veterinary clinic to help get your cat accustomed to trips in the car and the clinic environment.
  2. Get your cat used to being handled. Manipulate his paws, inspect his ears, clip his nails, open and inspect the inside of his mouth, move your hands over his legs and body and comb or brush his coat. If you do this regularly your cat will be less stressed when it’s the real thing at the vet’s office.
  3. Get your cat accustomed to a carrier. If the only time she sees the thing is for vet visits, you can’t blame her for panicking. Put her in the carrier with a few treats for five minutes a day for a week prior to the visit.

    Even consider feeding your cat in the crate, leaving the door open to encourage exploration on her own. Leave the carrier out for a week prior to the vet visit so she can inspect it. The morning of the appointment, find her well in advance of the time of your vet appointment and encourage her to enter the carrier on her own. Put an item with a familiar scent in the carrier, like her bedding or a favorite toy.
  4. Consider administering a natural calming agent like Bach Rescue Remedy or homeopathic aconitum prior to the visit. Talk with a holistic vet about specific homeopathic, herbal or nutraceutical remedies that might help address your kitty’s stress level.
  5. Keep your cool. Your kitty can sense your anxiety and stress, so remain calm. Stay positive and proceed at your cat’s pace. Tune in to how he’s responding, and use treats and other rewards to encourage desired behavior.

Sources and References

  • Royal Canin
  • 1 Banfield State of Pet Health Report, 2016 (Archived)
  • 2 Royal Canin News Release, August 18, 2016 (Archived)
  • 3 2011 AAFP/ISFM Feline-Friendly Handling Guidelines (Archived)

item.title: Why Vets Reach for This Vitamin in an Emergency
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Vitamin K1 (phytonadione) is the targeted antidote veterinarians reach for when a dog has been exposed to anticoagulant rat or mouse poisons. It restores the body's ability to activate the clotting proteins disrupted by the poison
  • Anticoagulant rodenticides are dangerously deceptive: A dog can look completely normal for three to seven days after exposure before serious internal bleeding shows up, which is why waiting for symptoms is one of the riskiest things you can do
  • Not all "vitamin K" is the same. K1 is the natural, plant-derived form used therapeutically; K2 is produced by gut bacteria and is linked to bone biology; and K3 is a synthetic compound used in feeds and is not interchangeable with the others
  • Treatment typically involves about 30 days of vitamin K1 therapy plus clotting tests, because "superwarfarin" rodenticides linger in the body for weeks, stopping early, even when the dog looks great, can let bleeding restart
  • Vitamin K is not a general-purpose blood booster; it won't treat anemia, low platelet counts, or inherited clotting disorders, and the over-the-counter version isn't equivalent to the prescription K1 that vets use; suspected rodenticide exposure is always an emergency-room conversation, not a home-treatment one

You discover a chewed-up box of rat poison behind the shed. Your dog seems fine, wagging, hungry, totally normal. So you take a breath and tell yourself it is probably okay. Then you call your vet and learn something you did not expect: This is exactly the kind of situation where every hour matters, and the treatment you might need is not a heavy-duty drug at all, but a vitamin.

Vitamin K, specifically vitamin K1, is one of the most important tools veterinarians have when a dog has been exposed to certain rat and mouse poisons. It is a quiet hero of the emergency-medicine world: low-drama, well-tolerated, and able to reverse a poisoning that would otherwise be fatal. Here is what is worth knowing about it.

What Vitamin K Actually Does

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for one critical job: helping the body make proteins needed for normal blood clotting. Clotting is the process that stops bleeding after an injury. It depends on a chain of proteins produced by the liver, and several of those proteins simply cannot work until vitamin K activates them.   • Vitamin K2 (menaquinone) is produced by gut bacteria and found in some fermented or animal foods. It’s often discussed in bone and calcium nutrition.
  • Vitamin K3 (menadione) is a synthetic vitamin K-active compound used in some animal feeds. It’s not interchangeable with K1 or K2.

After several days, the bleeding can become catastrophic, sometimes external, sometimes internal, and often hard to spot until things are very wrong.7

The poisons most commonly used today are sometimes called superwarfarins. They behave like prescription blood-thinner medications, but at much higher potency, and they can keep thinning the blood for three to five days or longer. That is why these poisonings are so dangerous: the effect builds quietly, and once severe bleeding starts, the window for intervention is small.8,9

Here is the part that catches a lot of pet parents off guard: A dog that has eaten anticoagulant rat poison usually looks completely normal in the first day or two. They may even seem fine for nearly a week.10

This is because outward signs of poisoning often do not appear until three to seven days after ingestion. By then, internal bleeding may be well underway. Possible signs include:11,12

  • Lethargy or sudden weakness
  • Pale gums
  • Difficulty breathing or coughing
  • Bloody stools or urine
  • Unexplained bruising or swelling under the skin
  • Nosebleeds
  • Prolonged bleeding from minor wounds
  • Vomiting, sometimes with blood
  • Collapse

Vitamin K1 works by going around the poison's blocked recycling pathway and supplying the body with a fresh source of usable vitamin K. With enough K1 on board, the liver can resume making functional clotting proteins, and the bleeding risk is brought back under control.13

It is a beautifully targeted treatment. The poison removes the body's ability to activate clotting proteins. The antidote replaces what the poison disabled. There are not many antidotes in veterinary medicine that work this cleanly.

Reports of vitamin K1 overdose in dogs are very uncommon, especially when it is used under veterinary supervision. Its synthetic cousin, vitamin K3, has a less favorable safety profile and is not used for this purpose. That is part of why the form matters so much, and why over-the-counter vitamin K supplements are not an equivalent product.14

What Treatment Looks Like

Treatment depends on how recently the dog ate the poison, how much was eaten, and which active ingredient was involved. A typical approach can include:

  • Decontamination — If exposure was recent (usually within a couple of hours), your vet may induce vomiting and give activated charcoal to limit absorption.
  • Vitamin K1 therapy — This is the heart of the treatment. K1 may be given by injection initially, especially if the dog is already symptomatic, and then continued as oral tablets or capsules at home.

    Because superwarfarins linger in the body for weeks, vitamin K1 is typically given for about 30 days. Stopping early, even when the dog looks great, can cause bleeding to restart.
  • Bloodwork and clotting tests — Your vet will likely check clotting times during and after treatment to confirm the therapy is working, and the body has cleared the poison.
  • Supportive care — Dogs who are already bleeding may need IV fluids, plasma, or even a blood transfusion to stabilize them while the vitamin K does its job.

Remember: Do Not DIY This

The form of vitamin K1 used to treat anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning is not sold over the counter. It requires a veterinary prescription, and the dose, route, and length of treatment all depend on the type of poison and the dog's clotting status.

Casual vitamin K from a supplement aisle is not the same product, is not dosed for this purpose, and may not contain the right form. Worse, it can give pet parents false confidence and delay the urgent veterinary care that actually saves lives.

And not all rat poisons work the same way. Some affect the nervous system or calcium balance instead of clotting, and vitamin K1 will not help with those. That is another reason the product label, the exposure timing, and a vet's evaluation all matter.15

  • Collect any packaging or bait you can find. The active ingredient on the label tells the vet exactly what they are dealing with.
  • Note when the exposure may have happened and roughly how much your dog may have eaten.
  • Call your vet, the nearest emergency hospital, or an animal poison hotline immediately; do not wait for symptoms to appear.
  • Do not try to induce vomiting at home unless specifically instructed to do so by a professional.
  • Bring your dog in for evaluation, even if they look completely fine.

Pet Poison Helpline (855-764-7661) and the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center are good resources to keep saved in your phone.

Vitamin K1 emergencies are the most dramatic story, but vitamin K also matters in everyday biology. Healthy dogs eating complete, balanced diets generally get enough vitamin K from their food and from compounds produced by gut bacteria.   • Liver disease or bile flow problems
  • Long-term gastrointestinal disease
  • Prolonged antibiotic use that disrupts gut bacteria
  • Homemade or incomplete diets
  • Unexplained bruising or abnormal clotting tests

One more thing worth knowing: Vitamin K is not a general-purpose blood booster. It will not raise red blood cell counts or treat anemia from other causes. item.title: This Beautiful Pet Will Favor Your Lap Over Most Anything Else
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Himalayan cats are a hybrid breed developed by crossing the Persian and Siamese breeds
  • “Himmys” as they are often called, are built more like Persians than Siamese and have the Persian temperament of preferring naps to exercise
  • If you’re thinking of adding a Himalayan to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations first to see if there’s an adoptable cat available
  • Himalayans are prone to health issues tied to their flat facial structure, including breathing difficulties, dental malocclusions, eye conditions and polycystic kidney disease
  • Daily grooming is important for Himalayans; their coat needs combing every day and a bath at least once a month

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 4, 2015.

Himalayan cats are a hybrid breed developed by crossing the Persian and Siamese breeds.

“Himmys” as they are often called, are built more like Persians than Siamese and have the Persian temperament of preferring naps to exercise. If you’re thinking of adding a Himalayan to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations first to see if there’s an adoptable cat available.

8 Cool Facts About Himalayan Cats

  1. Himalayans are hybrids


    The beautiful and unusual-looking Himalayan is a blend of the Persian and Siamese breeds and was developed through human intervention. Some cat fanciers think of the Himalayan as a distinct breed; others consider it a variety of the Persian breed.

    Himalayans have the characteristic flat, open faces of Persians. The eyes are a beautiful bright blue, and the ears are small and perky. There is a distinctive ruff around the neck that looks similar to a lion’s mane. Their bodies right down to their paws are large and fluffy.

    The Himalayan is often referred to as the “Himmy,” and has been called “a Persian in Siamese drag.”1
  2. Himalayans are built more like persians than siamese


    Despite the Himalayan’s Siamese lineage, he’s a medium-sized cat of 7 to 12 pounds, with a sturdy, muscular build and large bones.

    However, unlike this fellow in the tree, most Himalayans, in true Persian fashion, aren’t particularly active or athletic. Chances are you won’t find your Himmy doing much spontaneous leaping or climbing. He is unlikely to climb up your drapes, jump up on your kitchen counter, or scramble to the top of your refrigerator. Instead you’ll find him napping on a nice soft pillow, or even better, your lap.
  3. Himalayans are picky about who they bond with


    The Himalayan is a calm and somewhat reserved breed. They tend to share their affection and cuddles only with immediate family members, and they do best in a peaceful, low-key environment.

    Himmys shouldn’t be left alone for long periods of time, as they crave human contact and companionship.
  4. The himalayan’s coat is high-maintenance


    It’s extremely important that your Himalayan’s coat is groomed daily. It needs to be gently but thoroughly combed every day, and regular baths, at least monthly, are also recommended.

    Unfortunately, that luxurious coat also traps litter, especially in the paws. If the cat and her litterbox aren’t kept scrupulously clean, your Himmy is more likely than other breeds to just stop using the box.

    Other daily care should include wiping the corners of the eyes to prevent under-eye stains, and teeth brushing.
  5. Himalayans are prone to certain health conditions


    The Himalayan is an exotic breed with certain health problems primarily associated with their flat facial structure. These include difficult or noisy breathing, dental malocclusions, excessive tearing, eye conditions (e.g., cherry eye, entropion), hyperesthesia syndrome, and heat sensitivity.

    Other health problems of Himmys include polycystic kidney disease, and skin conditions.
  6. Himalayans are intelligent


    The Himmy is intelligent, although she’s not always given credit for her smarts. Challenge her brain by teaching her tricks and offering puzzle toys that reward her with treats when she learns how to solve them.
  7. Himalayans tend to get chubby


    Since your Himmy is by nature a lounger rather than an athlete, it’s important to feed him in way that will prevent him from growing overweight or obese. A balanced, raw, and species-appropriate diet made with organic, non-GMO ingredients, served in two portion-controlled meals per day is recommended.

    If you’ll be offering treats, make sure to factor those calories into kitty’s daily caloric intake.
  8. Himalayan kittens are often as mellow as adult cats


    Himalayan kittens are not quite as rowdy and rambunctious as many other breeds. Even very young Himmys typically have the gentle, mild temperament of an adult.

    Kittens often don’t look much like Himalayan adults. They are born a solid white or cream color and don’t develop their markings for a few weeks. It also takes time for their long, luxurious coats to grow in, and young Himmys don’t take on their full adult appearance until their second year.

Sources and References

  • iHeartCats.com, October 7, 2024 (Archived)
  • Cat Breeds Encyclopedia (Archived)
  • 1 Cattime.com

  • Chis tend to be one-person dogs who are fiercely loyal to their human

  • Chis are active, fun-loving little dogs that need daily exercise and close supervision both indoors and outside
  • If you’re thinking of adding a Chihuahua to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations for adoptable dogs

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 16, 2015.

Chihuahuas are one of the longest-lived breeds, despite their genetic predisposition to several health problems. Chis are active, fun-loving little dogs that need daily exercise and close supervision both indoors and outside.

If you're thinking of adding a Chihuahua to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations for adoptable dogs.

  1. The Chihuahua is the smallest dog breed in the world


    Even well-bred, healthy Chihuahuas are quite small, with average-size adults weighing just 4 to 6 pounds and standing a mere 6 to 10 inches high.

    Unfortunately, many disreputable people interested primarily in making money off their dogs deliberately breed Chis that will only weigh 1 to 2 pounds as adults. These dogs are advertised as "miniature" or "teacup," and while they may look adorable, they are typically very frail. Their bones are exceedingly thin and prone to sprains and breaks.

item.title: For Your Pet's Sake, Avoid These 2 Food Ingredients
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The pet food industry is constantly stressing the importance of fiber in dog and cat diets; however, canine and feline ancestral diets contain only minimal amounts of fiber
  • The fiber sources used in processed pet food are typically inexpensive fillers such as powdered cellulose (sawdust) and dried beet pulp
  • In dog and cat food, a small amount of fiber is very important, but a diet loaded with fiber is very detrimental
  • Pets eating commercial raw diets may need a source of species-appropriate fiber added to their meals
  • Pets with chronic loose or narrow stools may benefit from slippery elm bark — a soluble fiber that combines with digestive juices to produce a soothing gel that coats the GI tract and firms the stool

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 27, 2018.

The processed pet food industry continues to try to convince pet parents that dogs and cats need significant amounts of fiber in their diet.

This, of course, ignores the fact that canine and feline ancestral diets contain only minimal amounts of fiber or “roughage” (about 4% in the case of dogs) in the form of the hair, skin and teeth of prey animals, plus indigestible fibrous parts of plants and other odds and ends.

The popularity of grain-free diets has posed an ongoing problem for pet food manufacturers, forcing them to find alternatives to the inexpensive grains they’ve been loading up their products with for decades. As one pet food fiber ingredient supplier explains to its customers:

“As consumers demand grain-free diets, you must supplement your formulas with alternative fiber sources. This is where ingredients such as vegetable and fruit fibers, cellulose and beet pulp come in to play.”1

Of course, the reason processed pet food producers “must” use so much fiber in their formulas is because it’s plentiful and cheap. It has little to do with offering species-appropriate nutrition to dogs and cats. In the case of grain-free foods, it makes you wonder if the link between these diets and heart disease in dogs has been due in part to offsetting critical amino acids in meat with an overabundance of fiber and starch.

Fiber Sources Used in Processed Pet Food

The fiber ingredient supplier explains that fruit and vegetable fibers (which are typically byproducts — throwaways — from the human food industry) “can potentially provide added nutritional and health benefits for pets.” However, vegetable and fruit fiber is more expensive than “traditional” fiber sources used in pet food.

One of those “traditional” fiber sources is powdered cellulose, which is actually wood pulp (sawdust), primarily from pine trees. However, as the supplier points out, now that pet parents are looking for more natural ingredients in their pet’s diet, sawdust “just doesn’t fit the bill.”

In addition, powdered cellulose has a tremendous amount of insoluble fiber, and too much of it can interfere with your pet's ability to digest and assimilate important nutrients like protein and minerals. High levels of cellulose can also rob cells in the colon of critical fuel, like butyrate, due to reduced fermentation.2 Excessive powdered cellulose in your pet's food will also cause him to produce a bigger volume of poop.

According to the fiber supplier, beet pulp, a byproduct of sugar beets, is the second most widely used “traditional” fiber ingredient in processed pet food. Unfortunately, nearly 100% of all beet seeds produced in the U.S. are genetically modified, which is something else people don’t want to see in their pet’s food.

Plant Fiber Primer

Though fiber is indigestible and most types have no nutrient value, it does play an important role in the digestive process. The presence and type of fiber in the digestive tract determines how fast food passes through. Depending on the type of fiber, it can either speed up the process or slow it down.

Fiber increases bulk and water in the intestinal contents. It can slow down the rate at which food passes through the digestive tract in animals with too-fast transit times, and it can speed up the process in animals with slow transit times. That’s why fiber benefits both diarrhea and constipation.

Some fibers are also broken down in the intestine into fatty acids, which help prevent overgrowth of unfriendly bacteria. Fiber allows time for nutrients and water to pass from the large intestine into the bloodstream, and fiber also binds certain toxins in the gut and removes them from the body in feces.

Soluble fiber dissolves in water and is more digestible than insoluble fiber. Soluble fiber promotes smooth passage of food to the GI tract, while insoluble fiber speeds up the rate at which food passes through.

Soluble fiber sources include certain types of legumes, oats, rye, barley, some fruits and vegetables, root tubers, root vegetables, psyllium husk, flaxseeds and nuts. Insoluble fiber is also found in whole grain foods, wheat and corn bran, beans, peas, some nuts and seeds, as well as the skin of potatoes, lignans, green beans, cauliflower, zucchini and some fruits, including avocado, as well as the skin of some fruits, including kiwifruit and tomatoes.

Fibers are also fermentable and non-fermentable. A fiber is fermentable if the bacteria in the GI tract can break it down. Fermentable fibers contain nutrients that can be turned into energy for use by an animal’s body. Soluble fibers are generally more fermentable than insoluble fibers.

The types of fiber used most often in dry and canned pet foods include beet pulp, buckwheat and other grain hulls, flaxseed, fruit pectin, guar gum, oat and other brans, peanut shells, powdered cellulose, psyllium and tomato pomace.

Fact: Healthy Dogs and Cats Require Only Small Amounts of Species-Appropriate Fiber

When thinking about the need for fiber in your dog's or cat's diet, it's important to remember that wild canines and felines have no physiologic requirement for the plant fibers used in most processed pet food.

The fiber wild dogs and cats ingest is primarily derived from the already-digested stomach contents of their prey, plus fur, tendons and ligaments, along with nibbling grasses and other plant material. Although the amount of fiber in the diet of wild dogs and cats is small (less than 5% in most cases), it serves a very important role.

Dogs and cats fed processed commercial diets very often benefit from the addition of a small amount of the right kind of fiber, which is fiber that closely mimics the gastrointestinal (GI) contents of small prey animals. However, when your pet consumes unnecessary fillers, like wads of fiber, it inhibits digestion and absorption of many vital nutrients.

A small amount of fiber is very important, but a diet loaded with fiber is very detrimental. If you're feeding your dog or cat a nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate diet, which includes low-glycemic vegetables, along with appropriate supplementation, including pet probiotics and digestive enzymes, and she's easily producing small, firm stools, she's getting the amount of fiber she needs.

When Your Pet’s Diet Doesn’t Provide Enough Fiber

Several brands of commercially available raw food diets are constipating for some pets. This is due to the lack of fiber in the food.

Of course, opening a package of raw food to find hair, skin or guts would be totally disgusting. No one would buy such a product more than once, so it's understandable why raw pet food brands might be deficient in fiber content. The vast majority of balanced pet foods use low-glycemic, fibrous veggies to meet pets’ fiber needs naturally.

Veggies also provide much needed antioxidants and phytonutrients not found in meat, bones and organs. Without the benefits of veggies in raw food diets, pet run the risk of being constipated, as well.

In the wild, dogs and cats naturally choose how much grass to forage on and how much skin, hair and GI contents to consume with each prey animal they catch, but this isn’t true of pets living in domestic environments. This means sometimes they may need a little additional fiber for effective elimination, especially pets who are more sedentary.

If this is the case with your dog or cat, add extra ground leafy veggies to their meals — about a teaspoon for every 10 pounds of body weight, given once or twice a day. If that isn’t effective, you can try adding psyllium husk powder at one-half teaspoon for every 10 pounds of body weight, or coconut or organic acacia fiber at 1 teaspoon for every 10 pounds of body weight, once or twice a day.

If your pet is consistently producing narrow, loose stools, he may benefit from the addition of a soluble fiber called slippery elm bark to his food. When slippery elm combines with digestive juices, it produces a gel-like material called mucilage, which coats and soothes the GI tract and helps to firm the stool. About a half a teaspoon for every 10 pounds of body weight per meal should do the trick.

Additionally, canned or freshly steamed 100% pumpkin can also be very beneficial for these pets. About a teaspoon of pumpkin for every 10 pounds of body weight, one to two times a day, on the food can very effectively firm a loose bowel, and keep stools very regular.

Sources and References

  • 1 MFiber, Choosing the right fiber for the future of pet food
  • 2 PetfoodIndustry.com, September 12, 2016

item.title: Could That Burn Be Worse Than It Looks?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Burns in dogs are deceptive injuries — what looks like minor redness in the first few minutes can reveal itself as a much deeper wound a day or two later
  • The four main types — thermal, chemical, electrical, and mechanical — each call for slightly different responses
  • Burn severity depends on both depth and surface area, since widespread shallow burns can cause major fluid and protein loss and lead to systemic illness even when the wound looks less dramatic
  • Emergency first aid means cool water (not cold or icy) for 15 to 20 minutes, a loose nonstick covering, warmth for transport, and a fast call to the veterinarian
  • Even small-looking burns deserve a vet's eye, since the depth of injury may not be visible right away

Your dog leans against the wood stove for half a second. Your puppy nibbles a phone charger cord. A cup of hot coffee tips off the coffee table and lands on a curious nose. Whatever the scene, the panic hits fast — and what your dog's skin looks like in the first few seconds does not always tell the whole story.

Burns are deceptive injuries. The visible damage can be subtle at first, even when deeper layers of skin and tissue are seriously hurt. That is why even a small-looking burn deserves a careful look, and often a phone call to your veterinarian.

Why Burns Are So Easy to Underestimate

With most cuts and scrapes, what you see is more or less what you get. Burns do not play by the same rules. The skin's full response to a burn can take hours — sometimes days — to show up. Surface redness may not look alarming, but the tissue underneath can already be damaged.

That delayed reveal is especially true of thermal burns, where heat continues to penetrate even after the source is gone. By the time blisters form or the skin starts to darken, the burn has been quietly worsening below the surface. The early window for limiting damage is short.1,2

The 4 Main Types of Burns in Dogs

Most burns in dogs fall into one of four categories, and the type matters because the right response is not always the same. Here is what sets them apart:3,4

  • Thermal burns — They come from house fires, stoves, hot liquids, steam, hot pavement, sunburn, or radiant heat sources like wood stoves. These are by far the most common.
  • Chemical burns — They are brought on by contact with bleach, drain cleaners, battery acid, paint thinners, gasoline, or other harsh substances.
  • Electrical burns — Pets that chew on cords, become exposed to live wires, or when water becomes in contact with an electrical source. Mouth burns from cord-chewing puppies are a recognized type. Electrical burns can often lead to a dangerous build-up of fluid in the lungs, so the burns in the mouth are just the beginning.
  • Mechanical or friction burns — These result from friction, like rope burns, carpet burns, pavement burns, or leash burns when a dog drags or is dragged across a surface.

Knowing which type you are dealing with helps the veterinarian choose the right treatment — and in the case of chemical burns, it can change the very first step you take at home.

Severity Depends on 2 Factors

Burns are classified by how deep they go and how much of the body they cover. A small, very deep burn and a wide, shallow burn can both be dangerous, just in different ways. Burns covering a large surface area can cause major fluid and protein loss, leading to systemic illness even when the burn is not especially deep.5 In veterinary medicine, burn depth is classified under three categories:6,7,8

  • Superficial burns (first-degree) affect only the top layer of skin, the epidermis. You will see redness, swelling, fur loss, and tenderness. These typically heal in a few days with simple care.
  • Partial-thickness burns (second-degree) reach into the dermis, the second layer of skin. They are painful, often blistered, and may ooze or weep. These take a few weeks to a few months to heal and carry a real risk of infection.
  • Full-thickness burns (third-degree) destroy all layers of skin and the fatty tissue underneath. The area can look red, white, or charred and leathery black.

Because the nerve endings are destroyed, these burns can paradoxically feel less painful — which is one of the reasons they are easy to underestimate. Healing takes months, often requires surgical debridement or skin grafts, and leaves permanent scarring.

Emergency First Aid: What to Do (and What Not to Do)

If your dog has been burned, the first minutes count. Stay calm, and work through these steps in order:9,10

  1. Check the basics first — Make sure your dog is breathing and responsive, and call for emergency help if they are not. If you have been trained in pet CPR, this is where you use it.
  2. Cool the burn with cool (not cold) water — Run cool tap water over the area for about 15 to 20 minutes. This eases pain and helps stop heat from continuing to penetrate the deeper layers of skin. For a single burned body part, you can immerse it in cool water. Do not immerse a dog with widespread burns, as cooling too much skin too quickly can trigger shock.
  3. Cover the area gently — Place a clean, moist cloth or a sterile, non-adherent dressing loosely over the burn. The goal is to protect the wound from contamination, not to wrap or compress it.
  4. Keep your dog warm — especially with larger or deeper burns — A blanket draped over your dog during transport helps prevent hypothermia, which can sneak up quickly when significant skin is damaged.
  5. Use a muzzle if it is safe to do so — Even gentle, easygoing dogs can react unexpectedly when in pain. A makeshift muzzle from gauze or a soft leash can keep both of you safer on the way to the clinic.

Call your veterinarian or bring your pet to the emergency clinic immediately. Burns can worsen rapidly beneath the surface, and the sooner a professional sees the injury, the better the outcome. However, some old-school remedies actually make burns worse. Avoid the following:

  • Do not apply butter, petroleum jelly, oil, or human ointments — they can trap heat, contaminate the wound, and some are toxic to dogs.
  • Do not use ice or ice water — extreme cold can worsen tissue damage and cause hypothermia.
  • Do not pop or drain blisters — intact skin over a blister is actually protective.
  • Do not apply tight bandages. A loose, nonstick covering is what you want.
  • Do not immediately flush a chemical burn with water without checking first. Some chemicals react badly with water — look up the substance or call animal poison control before pouring.
  • Do not use peroxide, harsh soaps, or household disinfectants on a burn.

Does Every Burn Need a Vet?

Any burn that is deep, large, near the face or eyes, on the paw pads, or caused by a chemical or electrical source needs same-day veterinary care.

Even smaller, surface-level burns are worth a call to your veterinarian. As mentioned, what looks superficial in the first few minutes can reveal itself to be deeper a day or two later. A veterinarian can assess the depth of injury, prescribe appropriate pain control and antibiotics if needed, and give you specific instructions for at-home care.11

What Treatment Looks Like at the Clinic

Treatment depends on the type, depth, and extent of the burn. For mild burns, your veterinarian may simply clean the area, apply a topical treatment, and give you home-care instructions.

For more serious burns, treatment becomes more involved. IV fluids are often given to replace the fluids lost through damaged skin. Blood or plasma transfusions may be needed if protein loss is severe. Pain management is critical, since burns are notoriously painful — your veterinarian may use a combination of injectable and oral medications. Antibiotics are commonly prescribed for partial- and full-thickness burns to prevent infection.

Bandaging and topical treatments are tailored to the stage of healing, and bandages typically need to be changed daily under sterile conditions. For full-thickness burns, debridement and sometimes skin flaps or grafts may be needed to close the wound.

Dogs unable to stand may need help with positioning and nutritional support, since healing burns demand a lot of calories.12

Ongoing Care at Home

Once your dog is home, the work is not over. Your veterinarian will give you a specific care plan, but a few general principles apply:13,14,15

  • Watch closely for signs of infection — Increasing redness, swelling, warmth, foul odor, or discharge are all reasons to call back. Keep an eye out for areas turning black or leathery, which can signal the formation of eschar (dead tissue) that may need to be removed.
  • Keep your dog from licking, scratching, or chewing the area — A recovery cone or medical pet shirt can help. If bandages are part of the care plan, keep them clean and dry, and let your veterinarian handle the bandage changes when possible.
  • Only use topical products your veterinarian specifically recommends — Some over-the-counter options that work well for humans can be harmful to dogs, and others may slow healing rather than help it.

Reducing the Risk in the First Place

You cannot bubble-wrap every household risk, but a few habits can lower the odds of a burn happening in the first place. Take note of these safety reminders:

  • Use stove guards, fireplace screens, and baby gates to keep dogs at a safe distance from heat sources
  • Keep the kitchen a pet-free zone while cooking, especially with hot oil or boiling water
  • Run the hose for a minute before letting your dog drink — sun-warmed water inside the hose can reach scalding temperatures
  • Puppy-proof electrical cords and outlets — chewing on cords can cause mouth and palate burns, and lead to life-threatening pulmonary edema
  • Store bleach, drain cleaners, and other harsh chemicals well out of reach
  • Use dog-safe sunscreen on light-coated or thinly furred breeds
  • Watch hot pavement in summer — if the back of your hand cannot rest on the ground for seven seconds, it is too hot for paws

The Bottom Line

Dog burns can look minor in the moment and turn out to be much more serious as the hours unfold. Stay calm, cool the area gently, cover it loosely, skip the kitchen-cabinet remedies, and call your veterinarian — even for burns that seem small.

Most dogs recover beautifully from minor burns with prompt, calm care. The deeper or more widespread ones demand veterinary expertise and patience. Either way, your fast response and a clear-headed plan are what tilt the odds toward a smooth recovery and skin that heals as well as it can.

  • 2,4,8,10,11,15 American Kennel Club, October 7, 2025
  • 5 DVM360, August 1, 2008
  • 6,9,13 American Red Cross, Burns in Dogs
